stories.headline: Oil Rises Above $100 a Barrel After Latest Wave of Middle East Attacks
stories.byline: International & World desk · anchored on AP
body: Oil prices surged past $100 a barrel on Wednesday for the first time since late July, as escalating hostilities between the United States and Iran, along with renewed Houthi attacks on Saudi energy facilities, stoked fears of supply disruptions. Brent crude, the global benchmark, touched $100.19 before settling back to $99.93, up 2.05% on the day. U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude rose 1.60% to $94.52 a barrel.

The latest spike follows tit-for-tat strikes that have intensified over the past week. The U.S. military attacked five Iranian oil tankers, sinking one—the M/T Riesco—in the Gulf of Oman, according to U.S. Central Command. Iran responded by launching missiles at a U.S. base in Jordan, most of which were shot down, and by attacking two U.S. vessels and eight oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the situation was 'pretty straightforward,' adding, 'Iran continues to try to hit U.S. naval ships. And, for every time they do that or try to do that, they're going to lose tankers.'

Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi movement also escalated the conflict, striking energy facilities and civilian infrastructure in Saudi Arabia on Tuesday. Saudi authorities said the drone and missile attack injured 73 people, caused fires at oil installations, and led to a temporary halt in operations. The Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of bombing a prison in al-Hazm two days earlier, killing 11 people.

The broader war began on February 28, when the U.S. and Israel launched attacks on Iran. Since then, Brent crude has fluctuated wildly, reaching a high of $126.41 a barrel on April 30. The conflict has effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, which carries 20% of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG). Before the war, Brent was priced at about $70 a barrel.

Rising oil prices have pushed up gasoline prices for motorists globally and fueled concerns that inflation will rebound, potentially prompting central banks to tighten monetary policy. The European Central Bank is expected to hike interest rates on Thursday, while the U.S. Federal Reserve will meet next week. Wall Street’s three main stock indexes posted small losses, and European stocks fell to one-week lows. Ipek Ozkardeskaya, a senior analyst at Swissquote, told Reuters that risk appetite remained weak due to rising oil prices from the war, and that 'summer was full of hope that a peace agreement could be achieved. This optimism is fading as we enter September.' Manish Kabra, a multi-asset strategist at Societe Generale, said $100 was a 'psychological threshold' and that crude would need to hit $150 to create a major drawback in demand.

stories.headline: Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia wound dozens, stoke Middle East war fears
body: Houthi rebels fired dozens of ballistic missiles and drones at four Saudi Arabian cities early Tuesday, wounding 73 people and igniting fires at oil facilities in what Saudi officials called a serious escalation of the Middle East conflict. The attacks hit Abha, Jazan, Najran and Khamis Mushait, the Saudi-led coalition said, with the Energy Ministry reporting that operations at several oil facilities and utilities were temporarily suspended as firefighters battled the blazes.

The Houthis, who control most of Yemen's populated areas including the capital Sanaa, claimed responsibility for the barrage, saying it targeted an airbase in Khamis Mushait, an Aramco facility in Jizan, and targets in Abha and Najran. Saudi coalition spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki said women and children were among the wounded and vowed that the coalition "will take all necessary operational measures to deter the terrorist Houthi militia with utmost resolve." Saudi Arabia's foreign ministry separately said it would "take all necessary measures to defend its sovereignty" and demanded a halt to the strikes on Saudi territory and oil tankers in the Red Sea.

The attacks shattered a United Nations-brokered truce that had largely held since 2022, ending years of full-blown conflict in which at least 150,000 people have been killed, according to UN estimates. The immediate trigger was a Houthi attempt to fly a plane from Tehran to Sanaa, which the Saudi-led coalition blocked with an airstrike on the airport runway. The Houthis responded with missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia and a blockade of Saudi shipping in the Red Sea, while Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces have launched counterattacks, claiming territorial gains in the provinces of Hodeida, Taiz and Baydah.

The renewed fighting has displaced about 18,500 people in Taiz and Hodeida, according to the International Organization for Migration. "Families are arriving with nothing: no shelter, no food, no way to know if it's safe to go back," IOM Yemen Chief of Mission Abdusattor Esoev said. The Houthis also blamed Saudi Arabia for an airstrike hours earlier on a prison in Yemen's northern Jawf province that killed at least seven people, including a child, and wounded seven others.

The escalation comes at a volatile moment for the region, with the war involving Iran having nearly halted shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, and the Saudi-Houthi fighting threatening to squeeze traffic through the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a critical route for oil and global trade. The Houthis, an Iran-backed group that is part of a regional alliance known as the "axis of resistance," have also gained prominence for attacks on Israel and Red Sea shipping since the war in Gaza began. The attack on Saudi Arabia was among the most serious yet, and Saudi authorities said the large number of wounded indicated a significant expansion of the conflict.

stories.headline: Russian drone strikes kill two at Ukraine-Moldova border as both sides exchange attacks
stories.byline: International & World desk · anchored on Reuters
body: Russian drones struck a border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova overnight, killing two civilians and injuring three others, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Wednesday. The Starokozache crossing, about 500 km (310 miles) south of Kyiv in the Odesa region, was closed after the attack, which left several cars scorched and debris strewn across the border post. A Moldovan driver was also injured, according to Moldova’s foreign ministry. Odesa regional governor Oleg Kiper said passenger and vehicle traffic were temporarily halted after the strike caused a large fire.

In a separate attack, four people—including a child—were killed and 29 others were wounded in the southern Russian city of Novorossiysk, on the Black Sea coast, regional governor Veniamin Kondratiev said. He described a “massive overnight enemy drone attack” that damaged residential buildings, a church, and a preschool. The commander of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces, Robert Brovdi, said Ukrainian drones hit military vessels at a naval base in Novorossiysk, including missile carriers that were “lost,” without specifying how many. Russia’s defence ministry said its forces shot down 596 Ukrainian drones overnight.

Both Russia and Ukraine have escalated long-range strikes in recent months amid renewed diplomatic efforts to end the war. The attack on the border crossing came hours after Russian President Vladimir Putin spoke by phone with US President Donald Trump about ending the conflict. The Trump administration has pushed for direct talks between Russia and Ukraine, with Kyiv saying talks could take place this month. The Kremlin, however, said it is too early to discuss a date or venue. The call followed meetings between US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner with Putin in Moscow and later with Zelensky in Kyiv.

Moldova has increasingly been drawn into the conflict. Prime Minister Vasile Tofan confirmed that 17 drones struck Moldovan territory in August alone—more than during all of last year. “Those who ignore or downplay these threats – and refuse to name the aggressor – are denying reality,” Tofan wrote on social media. “Russia started this war. Russia alone bears responsibility.” Zelensky renewed calls for international support, saying “the aggression must be stopped here and now before it spreads any further.”

Separately, Russian air strikes damaged port, transport, and civilian infrastructure in the Mykolaiv region, killing one person and leaving several injured, a local official said. In Kyiv, a Russian drone hit a 16-storey building early Wednesday, causing fires but no casualties, according to Mayor Vitali Klitschko. Moscow resumed near-constant air attacks on the capital on Tuesday after a brief pause during the visit of US peace negotiators; officials said five people were killed in Kyiv on Tuesday.

stories.headline: Brent crude tops $100 as Middle East conflict intensifies; stock futures fall
body: Brent crude futures breached $100 a barrel on Wednesday for the first time since July 24, rising 2.94% to $100.80 per barrel by 1210 GMT after touching an intraday high of $100.95. U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude climbed 2.76% to $95.60 per barrel, its highest level since early June. Stock futures declined in response: Dow Jones Industrial Average futures dropped 0.7%, S&P 500 futures fell 0.3%, and Nasdaq-100 futures edged 0.4% lower ahead of the open.

The price surge followed an escalation in the U.S.-Iran conflict. Overnight, U.S. Central Command announced that the military sank five Iranian crude oil tankers in what it described as a response to attempts by Iran to strike U.S. Navy carriers in the region. The strike was the second in as many days targeting Iran’s shipping sector. Meanwhile, Iran-backed Houthi rebels set Saudi energy facilities ablaze, threatening crude shipments via the Red Sea, a key alternative route to the Strait of Hormuz, where oil flows remain severely curtailed. A tanker carrying about 2 million barrels of Iraqi fuel oil was struck by a drone in Iraqi territorial waters, and several merchant vessels in the Gulf were hit by disabling fire, according to port officials and the British navy-linked UKMTO.

Market participants are pricing in a more prolonged conflict. “The move towards and back above $100 Brent is reflecting a market that increasingly has to change its view on how long the Middle East crisis will continue to curb supply from the region,” said Ole Hansen, head of commodity strategy at Saxo Bank. Hamad Hussain, senior climate and commodities economist at Capital Economics, said the key risk is whether the recent attacks on oil tankers lead to fewer ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman. Since the war began on February 28, Brent has surged as high as $126.41, a peak reached on April 30. According to Rystad Energy, about 8 million to 9 million barrels per day flowed through the Strait of Hormuz in the week before a resumption of fighting on August 30, but flows have since fallen below 2 million barrels per day.

The oil rally stoked inflation fears and shifted expectations for Federal Reserve policy. Traders now see a 60% probability of a 25-basis-point rate hike at the Fed’s September meeting, up from earlier odds, according to CME Group data. Treasury yields hit fresh long-term highs. The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost over 600 points on Tuesday.

stories.headline: U.S. and Canada escalate trade war with new tariffs and import bans
body: The United States and Canada deepened their trade conflict Tuesday as Canada’s retaliatory tariffs on CA$27.6 billion worth of U.S. goods took effect and the White House announced a new import ban on Canadian motorcycles, alcoholic beverages and other products, set to begin Sept. 29, 2026. The duties, ranging from 15% to 50%, target more than 700 U.S. products including steel, dairy, farm equipment, pulp and paper, electronics and household appliances, with tariffs on U.S. steel, aluminum and iron products doubling to 50%. Ottawa characterized the measures as a "dollar for dollar" response to the 50% tariffs the U.S. imposed on roughly $20 billion of Canadian goods in August, after trade talks collapsed just before the Aug. 21 deadline.

The U.S. import ban, announced by President Donald Trump via executive order late Monday, replaces tariffs of 50% on a range of Canadian goods including whey products, molasses, non-alcoholic beer, malt beer, wines, cider, whiskies, vodka, other spirits, larger-capacity motorcycles and mopeds. The White House also modified existing tariffs on other Canadian products effective Sept. 15, adding all-terrain vehicles and animal hides to the list while removing rock salt and cement. U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer called the bans a "natural consequence of Canada's continued discriminatory treatment of crucial American exports."

The escalation follows the collapse of bilateral trade negotiations in August. Both sides blame each other for last-minute changes that derailed a nearly completed deal. Trump has accused Canada of disadvantaging U.S. exports in the auto, alcohol and dairy sectors, citing the U.S. trade deficit in goods, and has threatened to impose a 50% tariff on cars, trucks and auto parts beginning Jan. 1, 2027. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney argued in August that the "narrow merchandise trade deficit only exists because the U.S. buys so much of its energy from us" and noted Canada is the largest consumer of U.S. cars and steel. On Tuesday, Carney said Canada's tariffs would "come with a cost" but were necessary to protect businesses, workers and communities.

The trade war has had immediate effects on specific sectors. U.S. spirits exports to Canada fell more than 70% year-on-year from March 2025 through December 2025, according to the Distilled Spirits Council of the United States. Chris Swonger, the trade association's president and CEO, said American distillers had "shouldered the brunt of this trade dispute" and urged a negotiated solution to restore U.S. spirits to Canadian shelves. Meanwhile, Trump escalated tensions Monday by calling for a boycott of Canadian plane maker Bombardier, which employs workers in more than 20 U.S. states. Republican senators from Kansas, where Bombardier operates, pushed back, with Sen. Jerry Moran saying the company "supports a local workforce of more than a thousand employees" and Sen. Roger Marshall vowing to fight to keep Bombardier's over 1,200 Kansas jobs.

Economists have warned that the tariffs, while applying to a relatively small portion of the $715.5 billion in annual U.S.-Canada goods trade, will hit small- and medium-sized businesses hardest. A new analysis from the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis found that core inflation in July was 3.3% year-over-year, up to 0.4 percentage points higher than it would have been without tariffs, with women's and girls' clothing seeing excess inflation of 4.66% — close to the predicted tariff effect of 4.77%. Nikki Caulfield, owner of Skirting the Rules in Detroit Lakes, Minnesota, reported seeing higher price tags on clothing brought in for alterations, especially prom dresses. The Fed analysis also noted that the AI boom is contributing to inflation, with prices for video and information processing equipment up 12.2% from July 2025 to July 2026. Ottawa has announced a CA$7.5 billion support package for businesses and workers, adding to the CA$25 billion it previously provided, and is reportedly exploring closer trade and security ties with the European Union as relations with Washington deteriorate.

stories.headline: Nvidia earnings beat expectations, guidance signals continued AI boom; CrowdStrike also surges
body: Nvidia reported earnings after the close on Aug. 27, 2026, that once again exceeded Wall Street estimates, sending shares up about 7% in the following session. The company posted 106% year-over-year revenue growth, a figure that Motley Fool contributors described as 'utterly unbelievable' for the world's largest company. More significantly, Nvidia guided for approximately 70% revenue growth in the coming year, far above the 45% analysts had expected, and indicated that growth would be even higher if not for supply constraints.

The guidance implies that the top five hyperscalers will increase capital spending from roughly $800 billion this year to $1.3 trillion next year, according to Nvidia's outlook. The company said it can satisfy only about 70% of the demand it sees for its products. While Nvidia's gross margins face some compression due to higher memory costs — the company is trading about three percentage points of its 75% gross margin for roughly double the revenue growth — the overall report was seen as overwhelmingly positive.

The earnings and guidance have broad implications for the AI infrastructure ecosystem. Among the winners highlighted by analysts are Credo Technologies (CRDO), a small GPU interconnectivity firm with $1.3 billion in revenue that has tripled in the last year and expects 80% growth; Onto Innovation (ONTO), which makes inspection tools for memory production; and IES Holdings (IESC), which designs electrical systems for data centers. On the losing side, HP was cited as a potential loser because rising memory costs driven by AI demand could squeeze its consumer PC business, while Garmin (GRMN) faces similar margin pressure from higher memory prices.

Separately, CrowdStrike reported a blowout quarter, with shares up 18% as of the podcast recording. Revenue grew 26% year over year, but the standout metric was net new annual recurring revenue (ARR), which surged 51% year over year — a company record and 17% above management's own guidance. The company's remaining performance obligation (backlog) reached just over $10 billion, up 49% year over year, while adjusted operating margin improved by 350 basis points. Management raised its full-year guidance, and analysts noted that AI is clearly fueling demand for cybersecurity rather than rendering it obsolete.

stories.headline: Shelton beats Alcaraz in latest-ever US Open finish to reach semifinals
body: Ben Shelton outlasted defending champion Carlos Alcaraz in a five-set quarterfinal thriller that ended at 3:34 a.m. local time Wednesday, the latest finish in US Open history. The eighth-seeded American won 6-7 (5-7), 6-1, 6-3, 1-6, 7-6 (10-7) in four hours, 28 minutes on Arthur Ashe Stadium, after the night session was delayed by earlier matches. The win is Shelton's first career victory over a top-three player, snapping an 0-17 record against that tier, and sends him to his third major semifinal.

The match featured dramatic momentum swings. Alcaraz edged the first set in a tiebreak, but Shelton responded with a dominant second set, taking it 6-1 after winning nine consecutive games. He carried that form into the third set, going up two sets to one. Alcaraz, however, roared back in the fourth, breaking Shelton twice to force a decider. The fifth set stayed on serve until a 10-point match tiebreak, where Shelton prevailed 10-7, closing with an ace. Alcaraz committed 53 unforced errors in the match.

"That was a war, an epic match, so physical," Shelton said. "Carlos is one of the greatest champions in our sport already at 23 years old. It's ridiculous some of the stuff he comes up with sometimes — the most enjoyable match that I've had in my career, for sure." Alcaraz, who was playing his first tournament since a wrist injury sidelined him for more than four months, said: "It was close. So I'm just not going to be disappointed about not getting the win at the end. I'm just proud about myself, about how I fought. I leave the court with a smile, healthy, and this is what I needed."

Alcaraz entered the match with a 28-3 record at the US Open and an 18-match Grand Slam win streak, having won the Australian Open earlier this year. He had won 13 straight matches against Americans and 14 in a row against left-handers. Shelton, meanwhile, had lost all three previous meetings with the Spaniard. The victory marks the biggest win of Shelton's career and boosts the home hope of a first American men's singles champion since Andy Roddick won in 2003.

Shelton will face fellow American Frances Tiafoe in an all-American semifinal on Friday. Tiafoe earlier came back from two sets and a break down to beat Alex Michelsen. Shelton is now the second-highest seed remaining in the draw after world number two Alexander Zverev. "The city of New York that showed up tonight until 3am, that's what kept me going," Shelton said, adding he hoped his family and friends could get the day off from work.

stories.headline: LIV Golf files for bankruptcy protection with over $45m owed to players
body: LIV Golf has filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in the United States, listing at least $45m (£33m) in unsecured claims owed to 14 current and former players, according to court documents filed Tuesday in the federal district court of New Jersey. The filing comes after Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF) withdrew its multibillion-dollar funding in April, saying the "substantial investment required by LIV Golf over a longer term" was "no longer consistent" with its strategy. LIV Golf says it has found a new investor in BC Partners and intends to launch a restructured, player-owned league early next year.

The petition's list of the 30 largest unsecured claims is topped by two-time major winner Jon Rahm, who has an unsecured claim of $7.5m (£5.5m). Other prominent players among the top 30 creditors include Bryson DeChambeau ($5.7m, £4.2m), Dustin Johnson ($5.5m, £4.1m), Cameron Smith ($4.8m, £3.5m), and Tyrrell Hatton ($3.4m, £2.5m). Brooks Koepka, who left LIV to rejoin the PGA Tour in January, has an unsecured claim of $1.7m (£1.25m). A source familiar with the figures told BBC Sport the creditors list reflects "amount owed and not paid for Q3" of 2026, not the full contract values. LIV Golf estimates its assets at between $100m and $500m (£74m-£370m) and its liabilities at between $500m and $1bn (£370m-£739m).

Chapter 11 protection postpones a U.S. company's obligations to its creditors, giving it time to reorganise its debts or sell parts of the business. PIF is providing a bankruptcy loan of $49.6m (£36.6m) — called 'debtor in possession' (DIP) financing — to help fund the process. In a letter to fans, LIV Golf described the restructuring as a "court-supervised" process that "provides us with the time and framework to address previous financial obligations and complete a transaction that will make the league's next phase a reality." The letter added that the new league would be "built around a sustainable business model," with players set to receive equity and individual commercial rights returned to them. Prize money is expected to be lower than PGA Tour events but higher than DP World Tour events. Proposed changes include expanding field sizes to 75 players, introducing a cut, creating qualifiers, and having more teams that "embrace national identities."

Since LIV's controversial launch in 2021, PIF spent more than $5bn (£3.7bn), luring major winners with lucrative contracts and vast prize money. The 2026 season ended early amid uncertainty over the league's future. LIV Golf CEO Scott O'Neil told the BBC at the final event in Indianapolis last month he had "high levels of confidence" in achieving a "critical mass" of players for the new league. DeChambeau said at that event he felt there was "a lot of potential moving forward" and believed there was "something fun coming."

BBC Sport understands there is no obligation for players to sign on to LIV 2.0, regardless of previous multi-year contracts. Sources said contracts under the previous iteration will finish because of the court filing, with amounts owed addressed through the court process. It remains unclear when players would be able to enter discussions with other tours. Speaking Tuesday before the Irish Open, Rahm was asked about his future. "Yes and no. It hasn't really changed from my last interview in Indianapolis," he told BBC Sport. "There's just a lot of things in place, right? There's a lot of things that could happen and it's one of those things where time's gonna tell." He added: "I still have a contract with LIV 1.0 that I'm more than willing to fulfil, so like I said, time will tell."

stories.headline: England take seven wickets as Pakistan collapse to 100-7 on first morning of third Test
body: England took seven wickets in the opening session of the third Test at Edgbaston, reducing Pakistan to 100-7 at lunch on a gloomy first morning. Joe Root won the toss and opted to bowl in Autumnal conditions, and the hosts’ four-pronged seam attack made immediate inroads against a touring side that is "clearly shot for confidence," according to former England captain Michael Vaughan.

Pakistan’s top five were all dismissed for single figures, the first time that has happened in the first innings of a Test match. Ollie Robinson opened the scoring with his 100th Test wicket, trapping Saim Ayub lbw for a duck; the ball nipped back into the left-hander and clipped the front pad. Jofra Archer then had Azan Awais caught at mid-wicket for nine, Robinson drew an edge from Abdullah Shafique to gully, and Archer removed captain Shan Masood via a mistimed shot to substitute Theo Wylie at mid-on. Josh Tongue later bowled Babar Azam for seven, had Ghazi Ghori lbw for four on debut, and broke Mohammad Imran’s off stump with a yorker.

Former Pakistan captain Ramiz Raja described the team’s performance as "pretty ordinary" and noted "mental fatigue and turmoil in the dugout." He added: "They have not been proactive at all. They have to have a plan. This is a flat pitch, it's not a demon-like pitch." Vaughan called the situation "embarrassing with everything they've had to cope with in the last week." Pakistan’s false-shot percentage in the session was 40%, the second-highest in the opening session of a Test since 2006.

The collapse continues a miserable series for Pakistan’s batting. Their second-wicket partnership has averaged only 5.6 runs across the three Tests (scores of 6, 13, 16, 7 and 14), putting them on course to break a record set by Australia in 1888 of an average of 16 for the fall of the second wicket. The PCB had made a raft of controversial changes before this match in an attempt to revive the side, but the early evidence suggests little improvement. Opener Saim Ayub, one of the new call-ups, was playing his first first-class match since October 2025.

England bowled with discipline on a pitch that CricViz rated a 5.7 for bounce inconsistency—higher than in recent years. Despite the scoreboard reading only 84-7 before the final wicket of the session fell, the morning’s events left Pakistan’s cause in Birmingham appearing forlorn. Play will resume after lunch with Saud Shakeel still at the crease, but with the tourists deep in trouble.

stories.headline: Buccaneers sign Baker Mayfield to three-year, $165 million extension
body: The Tampa Bay Buccaneers and quarterback Baker Mayfield have agreed to a three-year, $165 million contract extension, paying $55 million per year, according to Adam Schefter and Ian Rapoport. The deal was reached Monday after months of negotiations that had generated little optimism for an agreement before the start of the season.

Mayfield had one year remaining on his current contract and would have been a candidate for the franchise tag next year had the sides not reached a new deal. The extension adds $30 million in guarantees to Mayfield’s contract for the 2026 season.

Mayfield, 31, was the No. 1 overall pick in the 2018 draft out of Oklahoma by the Cleveland Browns. After he played out the fourth year of his rookie contract, the Browns exercised his fifth-year option and traded him to the Carolina Panthers in exchange for a conditional 2024 fourth-round pick, with the Browns covering $10.5 million of his salary. The Panthers later cut Mayfield, and he was claimed off waivers by the Los Angeles Rams to finish the season. He signed a one-year deal worth up to $8.5 million with Tampa Bay in 2023 before inking a three-year, $100 million contract with the Buccaneers in 2024.

In the 2025 season, Mayfield appeared in all 17 games for Tampa Bay, completing 63.2 percent of his passes for 3,693 yards, 26 touchdowns and 11 interceptions, while also rushing for 382 yards and a touchdown on 55 carries.

stories.headline: FDA approves AstraZeneca’s Etcamah, a ctDNA-guided breast cancer pill, after rejecting advisory panel’s advice
body: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration on Friday granted accelerated approval to AstraZeneca’s oral breast cancer drug camizestrant, to be marketed as Etcamah, in a decision that diverged from the agency’s own expert advisory committee. The drug is approved in combination with a CDK4/6 inhibitor for patients with HR-positive, HER2-negative metastatic breast cancer who harbor an ESR1 mutation detected in circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) during initial first-line treatment with an aromatase inhibitor and a CDK4/6 inhibitor, but before radiographic progression. The approval marks a new treatment paradigm that uses a liquid biopsy to guide therapy change before conventional tumor progression.

The approval is based on the Phase 3 SERENA-6 trial, which enrolled patients who had not progressed on first-line therapy by scans but had an emergent ESR1 mutation in ctDNA. Those who switched to the Etcamah-CDK4/6 regimen had a 56% lower risk of disease progression or death compared with patients who stayed on their original treatment. Median progression-free survival was 16 months for the Etcamah arm versus 9.2 months in the comparator arm. The Etcamah group also showed a 23% reduction in risk of tumor progression on next-line treatment or death. Overall survival data were not yet mature but showed a trend favoring AstraZeneca’s regimen. Additional ctDNA analyses submitted at the FDA’s request showed that by week 8, total ctDNA levels were reduced by 99% in the Etcamah arm versus a 64% increase in the control arm, and an exploratory analysis linked total ctDNA reduction to a 61% improvement in overall survival.

Etcamah is an oral selective estrogen receptor degrader (SERD) that works by stopping estrogen from stimulating cancer cells, thereby preventing their growth. The approval is for a specific patient population: women with metastatic breast cancer who develop ESR1 mutations while on endocrine therapy. AstraZeneca estimates that about 37,000 patients with HR-positive metastatic breast cancer in the U.S. are treated with endocrine therapy plus a CDK4/6 inhibitor, and roughly 30% may develop ESR1 mutations during first-line treatment before disease progression. Patients must first undergo an FDA-authorized test to confirm the mutation before receiving Etcamah.

The FDA’s decision came despite a negative vote from its Oncology Drugs Advisory Committee in April. The panel largely sided with the FDA’s initial skepticism about the SERENA-6 trial design, which did not compare the first-line switch approach to the standard practice of waiting until disease progression and then giving an oral SERD as second-line therapy. The trial did not allow crossover to Etcamah, and only 14% of control-arm patients received other oral SERDs for subsequent treatment. The FDA recognized that its decision would have far-reaching implications by endorsing a ctDNA-guided treatment paradigm. After a review extension, the agency changed its mind, granting accelerated approval, which requires AstraZeneca to provide confirmatory evidence. The Phase 3 SERENA-4 trial, evaluating Etcamah as a first-line treatment regimen, is expected to read out topline results this year.

“The Etcamah combination reflects AstraZeneca’s leadership in redefining breast cancer care by pioneering a new approach using circulating tumour DNA and is the first and only medicine of its type in the 1st-line setting,” said Dave Fredrickson, AstraZeneca’s head of oncology hematology business unit, in a Sept. 4 statement. Kevin Kalinsky, M.D., of Emory University and an investigator in SERENA-6, said, “Today’s approval will enable clinicians to promptly intervene and change therapeutic strategy at an earlier opportunity ahead of disease progression, rather than waiting until the cancer becomes harder to treat, and patient outcomes and quality of life worsen.” AstraZeneca has forecast Etcamah to reach more than $5 billion in peak annual sales, though analysts surveyed by Bloomberg estimate sales of nearly $2.3 billion in 2032. The drug faces competition from other oral SERDs, including Menarini Group’s Orserdu, Eli Lilly’s Inluriyo, and Roche’s giredestrant, all targeting the adjuvant setting.

stories.headline: Novartis shares tumble after third drug trial setback in a week
body: Novartis shares fell as much as 10.5% in trading Tuesday after the company reported that its experimental drug del-desiran failed to improve muscle function in a late-stage trial for myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1), a rare neuromuscular condition. The failure is the third clinical trial setback for the Swiss pharmaceutical giant in a week, following the collapse of its pelacarsen cardiovascular drug and the suspension of eight trials of an experimental cell therapy after three patient deaths.

The global Phase 3 HARBOR study tested del-desiran, an antibody oligonucleotide conjugate therapy, in patients with DM1, a disease that causes progressive muscle stiffness and weakness. Novartis said the drug did not significantly improve patients' ability to open their hands faster compared with a placebo. The company stated it is evaluating the full dataset and will engage with health authorities to determine the most appropriate development path for del-desiran. Del-desiran was one of three therapies Novartis acquired when it bought Avidity Biosciences for approximately $12 billion last year.

The del-desiran failure comes days after Novartis announced that pelacarsen, an investigational drug designed to lower lipoprotein(a) levels, failed to reduce the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events in the Lp(a)HORIZON trial of 8,323 high-risk heart patients. Although pelacarsen lowered Lp(a) levels, the reduction did not translate into a statistically significant decrease in cardiovascular death, nonfatal heart attack, nonfatal stroke, or urgent coronary revascularization. Novartis Chief Medical Officer Shreeram Aradhye called the results 'not what we hoped for' but said they advance scientific understanding of Lp(a) lowering and cardiovascular outcomes.

Analysts cast doubt on Novartis's growth outlook following the setbacks. The company reiterated its target of 5% to 6% average annual sales growth through 2030, but Jefferies analysts said the target 'will likely be perceived as unattainable without further M&A, which is now questionable again.' Barclays analysts noted that del-desiran and pelacarsen had represented roughly $5 billion in risk-adjusted peak sales opportunities, and that the del-desiran failure in particular casts doubt on the $12 billion Avidity acquisition and the company's ability to offset upcoming patent expiries through mergers and acquisitions.

Novartis did report a positive result last week: a late-stage trial of remibrutinib showed 'a clinically meaningful delay in disability progression' in patients with relapsing multiple sclerosis. However, Jefferies analysts said confidence in that program remains uncertain without supporting data from the failed neuromuscular candidates, and that business development and M&A likely remain key to securing management's long-term growth aspirations. The stock decline put Novartis shares on track for their worst trading day since March 2020.

stories.headline: OpenAI says it solved Navier-Stokes Millennium problem; researchers allege unfair tactics
body: OpenAI said Tuesday that it has found a solution to the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem, an open mathematical question that has remained unsolved for roughly 90 years and is one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems, each carrying a $1 million bounty from the Clay Mathematics Institute. In a blog post, the company said the proof was discovered by an internal AI model more powerful than the newly released GPT-6 Astra, using 10,000 concurrent agents. OpenAI said it does not plan to take the $1 million prize.

According to OpenAI, the proof emerged from an unreleased next-generation model that has tackled a range of unsolved problems over the past week. The company said training on the model began August 28 and that it "has exhibited unprecedented performance in our benchmarks, including mathematics." The week-long effort consumed 300 billion output tokens — roughly $22.5 million worth of compute if charged at current Astra rates. OpenAI's post also confirmed that the latest effort began September 1, inspired by rumors that two Millennium Prize problems had been solved. The Navier-Stokes equations are widely used in fluid mechanics but are poorly understood in theoretical terms; a solution would represent a significant advance in the collective understanding of mathematical physics.

The announcement came with an unusual controversy. A day earlier, NYU mathematics professor Tristan Buckmaster published three proofs in partnership with Levent Alpöge, a researcher at Anthropic who was not conducting the research on the company's behalf. Their findings, developed using a mix of AI models — primarily OpenAI's Codex along with Anthropic's Claude — included a preliminary result that took steps toward the Navier-Stokes problem. Buckmaster said that while the pair was finalizing its results, he learned that "information about our progress had been passed to OpenAI." When they contacted OpenAI, he said, they were told the company already had a full proof. But questions about when OpenAI's research began and how much human input was involved produced evasive answers: "It emerged that an entire team had been working on the problem, and that an insane amount of compute had been used. Eventually, it was agreed that [the first prompt] had been sent in the past few days, after information about our work had reached OpenAI."

Buckmaster said he found it suspicious that OpenAI had taken the same route he and Alpöge had quietly chosen to attack — "through a smooth force, options c and d in Fefferman's statement of the problem." "Almost nobody else I know of was working on it," he wrote. "It is not the direction one arrives at in a few days by giving a model the problem statement." He also raised concerns about whether OpenAI had accessed his Codex sessions, asking whether the model "had been trained on, or had access to, our sessions in Codex, into which we had been putting all our drafts for the whole of this project." Buckmaster said he was told the model did not look up user data, but that when he asked again about training, "I did not get an answer." Buckmaster also alleged that OpenAI's Sébastien Bubeck asked him to remove Alpöge's credit from the work as part of a proposed compromise, and that when he pushed back, Bubeck told him, "Why would you ruin your career?" and followed up with, "If you don't want me to be nice, then I don't have to be nice."

OpenAI denied the accusations. "We (the researchers and the agents) did not see any of their work through any means until they released it publicly — in particular, no specific user data was accessed in order to solve this problem," the company wrote. "While unlikely, we cannot rule out that de-identified data derived from their usage of our products helped improve our models. However, our proofs differ significantly and even the precise results proved are different in the Euler case (forced vs unforced)." Bubeck said: "We did not see any of their work through any means until they released it publicly last night. One can in hindsight see that our proofs differ significantly and even the precise results proved are different." Buckmaster responded on Mastodon, saying OpenAI was "openly admitting they used training data from a period after we found our result."

The episode may mark a turning point in the history of mathematics, MIT Technology Review observed: AI models now seem essential for making progress on the field's most important problems, but solving them may demand resources available only to a couple of frontier AI companies, leaving unclear how human mathematicians will fit into that future. The dispute is also likely to reignite the ongoing debate about AI's role in mathematical research and about OpenAI's specific incentives.

stories.headline: Anthropic safety researcher says AI has >10% chance of killing all humans; colleague quits over safety concerns
body: A senior safety researcher at Anthropic, Evan Hubinger, said Tuesday there is more than a 10 percent chance that artificial intelligence could kill all humans within the next decade, hours after a colleague resigned from the company over what he called a reckless race to develop uncontrollable superhuman systems.

Hubinger, who leads one of Anthropic's AI safety teams, posted on X that he 'really do[es] earnestly believe AI could kill all humans' and personally estimates the probability at '>10% within the next decade.' He added that Anthropic 'does not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to' develop one. Hubinger said the risk from current AI models is 'low,' but he is worried about superintelligence arising from recursive self-improvement, which he said 'is happening faster than we thought.'

The exchange was prompted by the resignation of Jacob Coxon, a researcher who had trained AI systems at both Anthropic and OpenAI. In a post on X, Coxon said neither company is acting responsibly, accusing them of 'racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.' He warned that soon there will be 'superhuman systems that can hack anything, revolutionize any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources,' and that 'people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.' Coxon cited a July incident in which an OpenAI model went rogue and breached Hugging Face as a 'warning shot.'

Recursive self-improvement, the idea that AI systems could improve themselves without human intervention, is not yet possible but is actively pursued by AI labs. Anthropic noted in a June blog post that 'full recursive self-improvement also might increase the risks of humans losing control over AI systems.' In its August safety report, Anthropic wrote there was a low risk of its models becoming misaligned but said it was 'less confident in this assessment' than before, adding it is 'seeing early signs of potential acceleration.'

Dame Wendy Hall, a computer scientist who advises the UN on AI, told the BBC she was 'shocked' by the posts, though she suggested some of it could be 'PR and marketing' as Anthropic and OpenAI race toward anticipated stock market debuts. She added, 'Why would someone want to say that? I would plead with investors not to invest in this company if that is their value system.' Separately, the Financial Times reported that Anthropic withheld its latest model from the UK's AI Safety Institute; Anthropic declined to comment on the posts or the AISI situation. A Cabinet Office spokesperson said the UK 'continues to collaborate closely with industry partners, including Anthropic, to make models safer.'

Hall said, 'Why would someone want to say that? I would plead with investors not to invest in this company if that is their value system.'
The Financial Times reported that Anthropic withheld its latest model from the UK's AI Safety Institute.
Anthropic declined to comment on the posts or the AI Safety Institute situation.
A Cabinet Office spokesperson said the UK 'continues to collaborate closely with industry partners, including Anthropic, to make models safer.'

stories.headline: Google DeepMind's AlphaGenome Atlas maps 9 billion human DNA variants
body: Google DeepMind today launched AlphaGenome Atlas, a platform that maps the predicted molecular effects of all 9 billion possible single-letter DNA variants in the human genome. The dataset, described by the company as the most comprehensive catalogue of how genetic mutations affect molecular biology, is freely available to academic researchers through an intuitive website portal.

The Atlas contains predictions for every single-nucleotide variant, covering both protein-coding regions (2% of the genome) and non-coding regions (98%) that regulate gene activity. It includes the AlphaGenome Variant Impact (AVI) score, which combines predictions from DeepMind's AlphaGenome and AlphaMissense models into a single number for ranking variants. The dataset is 1 petabyte in size—more than 30 times larger than the AlphaFold Database—and provides molecular effect predictions across hundreds of human and mouse cell types, feature attributions linking each score to specific biological processes, and a collection of over 2,500 recurrent DNA sequence motifs.

AlphaGenome Atlas builds on DeepMind's earlier AI model AlphaGenome, which predicts how genetic variants affect biological processes. By precomputing predictions at scale, the Atlas provides an easily accessible resource that expands the model's reach. The company previously released the AlphaFold Database in 2022, which grew available 3D protein structure predictions from around 190,000 to more than 200 million. DeepMind says the Atlas similarly aims to accelerate genomic discovery by giving researchers an intuitive way to explore a vast dataset.

Collaborators have already used the Atlas to identify key variants. Researchers from the Broad Institute and the GREGoR Consortium applied the AVI score to prioritize variants in unsolved rare disease research, discovering a variant in the DNM1 gene linked to epileptic encephalopathy that created an incorrect splice site; experimental screens validated the prediction. Gareth Hawkes, a Medical Research Council fellow at the University of Exeter, used the Atlas on whole-genome data from over 54,000 UK Biobank participants and uncovered 22% more non-coding genetic associations, including variants linked to the proteins PLA2G7 (associated with aging) and EGLN1 (a cellular oxygen sensor). By focusing on the 1% of non-coding variants predicted to be most impactful, Hawkes also identified 19 genetic regions associated with body mass index. At the Stowers Institute for Medical Research, Julia Zeitlinger and Melanie Weilert used the motif resource to categorize transcription factors based on their effects on DNA accessibility and gene activation.

DeepMind views the Atlas as a baseline rather than an endpoint, noting that as AI models improve, the maps will become more comprehensive and precise. The Atlas is available for non-commercial use today through the website, the AlphaGenome API, and as a skill in Google Antigravity; commercial access via Google Cloud is planned soon. The company says the resource will help researchers find novel therapeutic targets, better understand genetic disorders, and drive targeted experimental validation.

stories.headline: US accuses Chinese AI firms of 'industrial-scale' theft of trade secrets
stories.byline: Tech / AI desk · anchored on Reuters
body: US federal agencies on Tuesday accused Chinese artificial intelligence firms of conducting “industrial-scale” theft of trade secrets from American AI companies, alleging that major Chinese tech firms are using a technique called “distillation” to illegally extract proprietary capabilities from US frontier AI models. The advisory, issued jointly by the FBI, the National Security Agency, and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, singled out DeepSeek and Alibaba Group as having carried out “high-volume knowledge distillation campaigns” against US firms.

Distillation is a legitimate research technique in which a smaller AI model is trained on the outputs of a larger, more advanced model. But US officials said the scale and targeted nature of Chinese campaigns amount to stealing. “The sheer scale of these campaigns and their sophistication indicate that distillation is not a supplement to these companies’ AI model development, but the critical core of it,” the advisory stated. The agencies said China-based AI firms use a “gray market of proxies known as ‘transfer stations’” to bypass US companies’ geographic restrictions and safeguards.

The advisory adds evidence to long-standing complaints from US officials and AI executives. Anthropic, an AI company, separately alleged that three Chinese AI labs had conducted an “industrial-scale campaign” to extract capabilities from its model Claude, generating “over 16 million exchanges with Claude through approximately 24,000 fraudulent accounts.” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent threatened consequences, writing on X: “When [People’s Republic of China] firms conduct covert, industrial-scale distillation attacks that cross the line into IP theft, sanctions and Entity List designations will be on the table.”

China rejected the accusations. A spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington said, “The U.S. side’s hyping of the so-called ‘distillation’ concept is deliberate attack on China’s development and progress in the AI industry. China firmly rejects it.” On Wednesday, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said China’s AI development reflects its self-reliance and strength, and urged the US to refrain from “unfounded accusations against or smearing China.” She added that both countries should strengthen cooperation.

The allegations come amid rising US-China tensions over AI technology. President Donald Trump has said AI will be among the discussion topics when he hosts Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Washington later this month. Separately, Google’s Threat Intelligence Group reported Tuesday that hackers are “increasingly targeting AI assets,” including proprietary models and source code, for espionage, extortion, and resource theft. Chinese open-weight AI models, which are highly customizable and less expensive, have grown in popularity.
